client: I've been really stressed out lately because my final exams are next week and I honestly don't feel ready at all. I've been working so many hours at my part-time job just to cover rent that I've barely had time to study, and it feels like everything is piling up at once. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because at the end of the day the problem is just... time, and I don't have enough of it.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that you're feeling overwhelmed — you're genuinely juggling a lot of real, competing demands, and that exhaustion is valid. I also hear a little voice in there saying that talking won't help, and I'm curious about that thought, because sometimes when we're stretched thin, our minds convince us that *nothing* will help, which can make the weight feel even heavier. 

What would it feel like if, just for this conversation, we explored whether there are any small shifts — in how you're thinking about the situation or planning your time — that might create even a tiny bit of breathing room?

client: I guess I'm willing to try, but honestly, part of me is already bracing for the usual "make a schedule" or "practice self-care" advice that sounds good in theory but falls apart the moment my boss dumps three urgent projects on me at once. It's like, I already know what I *should* be doing, and yet here I am, still drowning. I don't know if a small shift is even possible when everything feels like it's on fire at the same time.
therapist: You're not wrong to be skeptical — generic advice that ignores your actual reality isn't helpful, and it sounds like you've already tried to "do the right things" only to have circumstances knock them over, which is genuinely frustrating. What I'm more curious about isn't adding things to your plate, but rather that feeling of *everything being on fire at once* — because sometimes when we're in that state, our brain treats every problem as equally urgent and equally unsolvable, which can make it hard to see if any one flame is actually smaller than it feels. When you picture all these fires right now, is there one that feels like it's burning slightly differently from the others — maybe one that's more about the situation itself versus one that's more about how you're *feeling* about the situation?

client: I guess... maybe the loneliness one burns a little differently. Like, the work stress and the financial stuff feel more like external fires that I can at least point to and say "that's the problem right there," but the loneliness is more like this slow, suffocating smoke that I can't quite locate the source of. It's harder to explain because it's not like something happened — it's more like nothing keeps happening, if that makes any sense.
therapist: "Nothing keeps happening" — that phrase is so beautifully and painfully accurate, and it makes complete sense that this kind of loneliness is harder to wrestle with, because there's no single moment to point to or fix. It's like your nervous system is quietly registering an absence over and over again, which can actually be more draining than the concrete stressors, even if it feels less "legitimate" to talk about. I'm wondering — when you imagine what the opposite of that suffocating smoke would feel like, even just a small version of it, what comes to mind?

client: I think the opposite would feel like... being in a room where someone actually notices when you walk in. Not in a big dramatic way, just like, someone's face changes a little because you're there. But even imagining that makes me feel kind of embarrassed, like I'm admitting to something pathetic.
therapist: That image you just described — someone's face changing simply because *you* walked in — is one of the most fundamentally human things a person can long for, and there is nothing pathetic about it whatsoever. The fact that even imagining it brings up embarrassment is worth being gentle with, because it tells me you might have somewhere along the way picked up the idea that needing to matter to people is a weakness, rather than just... being human. Where do you think that belief came from — the one that says wanting to be noticed is something to be ashamed of?

client: I don't know, maybe... growing up, I got the sense that needing people was a burden, like if you wanted too much attention you were being selfish or clingy. I remember my mom being really busy and I learned pretty early not to ask for too much, just kind of fade into the background so I wouldn't add to her stress. It's weird hearing you say it's just "being human" because part of me wants to believe that, but another part still feels like wanting that kind of connection is embarrassing, like I should be past needing it by now.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and it makes so much sense — a younger version of you learned that shrinking yourself was an act of love toward your mom, and that was actually a wise adaptation for a child trying to navigate a stressful home. The painful part is that the lesson your child-self learned ("my needs are a burden") is still running in the background now, making you feel embarrassed for wanting something that every human being genuinely needs. I'm curious — if a close friend told you they felt lonely and just wanted to matter to someone, would *you* think they were being selfish or pathetic?

client: I mean... no, of course I wouldn't think that about a friend. I'd probably want to help them, tell them their feelings make sense. But it's different when it's me — like, I can extend that understanding to someone else no problem, but when I try to turn it toward myself it just feels... fake, or like I'm making excuses for being needy.
therapist: You just noticed something really important — that the compassion flows easily outward but hits a wall when you try to turn it inward, and that gap is actually at the heart of so much of what you're carrying. That feeling of "fakeness" isn't proof that self-compassion is wrong for you; it's more likely just the unfamiliarity of it, like a muscle that was never really allowed to develop because you learned so early to need so little. I wonder — what do you think that younger version of you, the one who quietly faded into the background, would have needed to hear most?

client: I sat with that question for a second and it actually kind of caught me off guard, because my first instinct was to say "it doesn't matter what she needed, that was a long time ago." But then something quieter came up, like... maybe she just needed someone to notice her without her having to earn it first. That feels embarrassing to even say out loud, like I'm being dramatic or self-pitying, which I guess kind of proves your point about the wall.
therapist: The fact that your first instinct was to dismiss her — "that was a long time ago" — and then something quieter and truer surfaced anyway, that's not drama, that's actually a really courageous moment of honesty with yourself. And "noticed without having to earn it first" is such a precise and tender thing to name, because it sounds like so much of your life has been spent making yourself small or useful or undemanding just to feel okay about taking up space. I'm sitting with how that same little girl is still here, still waiting for that — and I'm wondering, in your life right now, is there anyone or any space where you feel even the faintest version of that, where you don't have to earn your place?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to say no, there's nobody. But then I thought of my cat, which feels almost embarrassing to admit, because it sounds pathetic compared to what you're describing. She just comes and sits on me, not because I fed her recently or was useful, just because she wants to be there, and I don't know, maybe that counts for something even if it's not a person.
therapist: That is not pathetic at all — that is actually a perfect, real example of exactly what you described needing, presence without conditions, and your cat has apparently been offering it to you all along. What's beautiful about this is that you *noticed* it, even through the embarrassment, which means some part of you is already capable of receiving that kind of unconditional connection even if it's still hard to let it in fully from people. I'm curious — when she comes and sits on you, what do you usually do with that moment, do you let yourself actually feel it, or does something in you tend to brush past it?

client: Honestly, I think most of the time I brush past it. Like, I'll notice it for a second, maybe even feel something warm, and then my brain just... moves on, starts thinking about whatever I didn't finish at work or some awkward thing I said to someone three years ago. It's like I can't just stay in the moment, something always pulls me back into my head.
therapist: What you're describing is so common and yet so quietly costly — your nervous system gets a tiny taste of warmth and safety, and then your mind, almost protectively, pulls you back into problem-solving or ruminating, as if stillness itself feels a little unsafe. It's almost like that same little girl who learned to stay small also learned to stay *busy*, because resting in a moment of being cared for was never really practiced or allowed. What do you think might happen — even just inside you — if the next time your cat settles on you, you let yourself stay with that warm feeling for just a few breaths longer than usual?

client: I think you're probably right that staying busy feels safer than just... sitting with something nice. But honestly, when I imagine actually trying that with my cat, there's this immediate worry that I'll just end up feeling sad instead of peaceful, like the warmth will remind me how lonely I usually am. It's like I'm afraid that letting myself feel it will make the absence of it everywhere else hurt more.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense, and it's actually a really insightful thing to notice — that opening the door to warmth feels risky because it also opens the door to grief, the grief of how much you've been without it. But I want to gently offer another way to look at it: the loneliness is already there, already hurting, whether you let yourself feel the warmth or not, so in a way you're currently paying the cost without receiving any of the comfort. I wonder — what would it mean for you if it turned out that you *could* hold both at once, the sadness and the warmth, without one canceling the other out?
